Let $\Omega$ be a complex domain and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be harmonic.

1. If $u$ has an interior local maximum or an interior local minimum, then $u$
   is constant on $\Omega$.
2. If $\Omega$ is bounded and $u$ extends continuously to $\overline{\Omega}$,
   then
   $$\sup_{\overline{\Omega}}u=\sup_{\partial\Omega}u,\qquad \inf_{\overline{\Omega}}u=\inf_{\partial\Omega}u.$$

Let $\Omega$ be a complex domain, let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be harmonic, and
let $v_1,v_2$ be harmonic conjugates of $u$ on $\Omega$. Then $v_1-v_2$ is a
real constant on $\Omega$.

derivations.claim: On each closed vertical substrip $\epsilon\le x\le a-\epsilon$ the summands and every fixed complex derivative are bounded by a polynomial in $k$ times $e^{-k\pi\epsilon/b}$. The series therefore converges normally there and defines a holomorphic function. Its imaginary part is zero on the open horizontal sides, where the same normal convergence applies. Put $q_1=e^{\pi(z-a)/b}$, $q_2=e^{-\pi z/b}$. The exact identity $$\frac{\sinh(k\pi(z-a/2)/b)}{\cosh(k\pi a/(2b))}=\frac{q_1^k-q_2^k}{1+e^{-k\pi a/b}}$$ shows that $p$ differs from $$\frac2\pi\log\frac{1+q_1}{1-q_1}-\frac2\pi\log\frac{1+q_2}{1-q_2}$$ by a function holomorphic in a neighborhood of the closed rectangle. Indeed the difference coefficients acquire the exponential factor $e^{-k\pi a/b}$, and its derivatives converge normally in a slightly larger rectangle. The logarithms here are the power-series branches in $|q_j|<1$, since $\sum_{k\text{ odd}}q^k/k=\tfrac12\log((1+q)/(1-q))$ by termwise differentiation and its value at zero. This proves analytic extension up to every side away from the four corners. [given, construct, algebra]

On either open vertical side the imaginary part of each hyperbolic quotient is $\sin(k\pi y/b)$. Thus its boundary value is one: for $0<\theta<\pi$, the identity in step 1.1 and its radial limit give $$\sum_{k\text{ odd}}\frac{\sin(k\theta)}k=\frac\pi4,$$ because $(1+e^{i\theta})/(1-e^{i\theta})=i\cot(\theta/2)$ has argument $\pi/2$. The exponentially convergent remainder in step 1.1 justifies the boundary passage, or equivalently first take radial factors and then the continuous analytic extension there. At each corner exactly one of $1\pm q_j$ has a simple zero. The same logarithmic formula gives the stated coefficient $\pm2/\pi$, with a holomorphic remainder. Its imaginary part is consequently bounded at each corner and ranges in $[0,1]+o(1)$ on small inward quadrant arcs; its two adjacent side values fix the additive imaginary constant. Apply [F1] to the rectangle with small corner disks removed and let their radii tend to zero. This gives $0\le\operatorname{Im}p\le1$, and the strong principle makes both inequalities strict inside, since the side values differ. Exponentiating the corner logarithm gives a nonzero linear coefficient in the corresponding end coordinate. Reflection across an open side follows directly by continuing the holomorphic logarithmic expression, or by its real/constant-imaginary boundary value. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

This map is proper into the open strip. A sequence leaving every compact subset of $R$ approaches an open side, where its imaginary part tends to zero or one, or a corner, where its real part tends to the appropriate infinite end. Thus no inverse image of a compact substrip set escapes. A nonconstant holomorphic map is open: its local Taylor expansion at any point is $p(z)-p(z_0)=c(z-z_0)^r(1+O(z-z_0))$, and a small-root argument, or a circle winding count, puts a small disk about $p(z_0)$ in its image. Properness makes its image closed in the strip: preimages of a converging image sequence remain in the inverse image of a compact disk about its limiting strip point, and have a convergent subsequence. Since the strip is connected, the image is the whole strip. For a fixed $t_0\in(0,1)$ and very negative real part, the only preimages lie near the southwest and northeast corners by compactness away from them. Their exponential end coordinates in step 2.1 each have nonzero derivative, so there is exactly one simple preimage there. The proper degree is therefore two. It is locally constant on regular target values by these local inverses and compactness; crossing a critical value preserves the total multiplicity by the displayed local power model. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Compactify the strip by its two corner coordinates $e^{\pi p/2}$ and $e^{-\pi p/2}$. It is a topological closed disk with two boundary corners. The four corner expansions make $p$ an unramified boundary map there, and reflection gives the same along its open sides. Interior critical points are finite: the derivative extends holomorphically and nonvanishingly in all the boundary charts, while its interior zeros are isolated in a compact remaining set. The degree-two cover has Euler defect exactly one. To verify this finite count, join its finitely many critical values to boundary points by a finite embedded planar tree, subdividing at intersections; equivalently use the explicit upper-half-plane coordinate $e^{\pi p}$ and its fractional linear disk coordinate to draw these finite arcs. Subdivide the resulting disk faces into finitely many triangles. Away from critical values every vertex, edge and face has two lifts. At a critical point of local degree $r$, the lifted vertex count is smaller by $r-1$, with no other defect. Hence $\chi(\overline R)=2\chi(\overline B)-\sum(r-1)$, or $1=2-\sum(r-1)$. Every summand is positive, so there is exactly one critical point and its local degree is two. This uses finite lifted cells, not an unproved global index theorem. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Finally let $p'$ be another map with the stated bounded imaginary part and side values. The bounded harmonic difference $h=\operatorname{Im}(p'-p)$ vanishes on all open sides. For each $\epsilon>0$ use the positive harmonic barrier $$B_\epsilon(z)=\epsilon\sum_c\log(C/|z-c|),$$ summed over the four corners, with $C$ larger than the rectangle diameter. It is positive throughout, diverges at the corners, and has no interior singularity. On the punctured rectangle with sufficiently small corner disks, boundedness of $h$ and its zero side values give $h\le B_\epsilon$ and $-h\le B_\epsilon$ on its boundary. Principle [F1] gives the inequalities inside. Let the corner radii tend to zero and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$ to obtain $h=0$. The holomorphic difference $p'-p$ has zero imaginary part and hence is a real constant by the Cauchy--Riemann equations, equivalently [F2]. This proves uniqueness with exactly the permitted translation freedom. All series, logarithms, finite cuts and limits above are explicit; no full-Choice extremal Riemann-mapping supplier was invoked. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

boundaries.reason: Rectangle dimensions a,b are strictly positive.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 2.1 handle convergence and exact zero/one side values.
Step 4.1 proves exactly one simple branch by finite Euler counting.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 give actual logarithmic corner expansions and nonzero end-coordinate derivatives.
Steps 2.1 and 3.1 distinguish both negative corners from both positive corners.
Steps 1.1 through 5.1 use explicit convergent series, finite cuts and harmonic barriers, not full-AC Riemann mapping.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $G$ be a knot grid of size $n\ge2$ on its actual flat torus, with horizontal alpha and vertical beta circles and the product-integrable end data. Let $u:x\to y$ be any REALIZED continuous Whitney class, with integral domain $D$. At a grid vertex $v$ write $\nu_v(D)$ for one quarter of the sum of its four adjacent cell coefficients, and put $n_x(D)=\sum_{v\in x}\nu_v(D)$. Then its actual fixed-end real index before translation is
$$\mu(u)=n_x(D)+n_y(D).$$
This includes signed domains and positive marked degrees. If every cell coefficient is nonnegative and $\mu(u)=1$, then $x,y$ differ in exactly two points and $D$ is exactly one embedded torus rectangle from $x$ to $y$, of multiplicity one and with no state point in its interior. No exclusion of $O$ or $X$ marks is imposed. Its row and column intervals are both proper cyclic intervals, so it is an ordinary rectangle among the four choices for those changed corners.

This proves actual index and domain classification, not existence or uniqueness of holomorphic representatives, their count, equality of equal-domain homotopy classes, or a grid-to-analytic chain equivalence.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $G$ be an oriented knot grid of size $n\ge2$, with its actual flat torus and product generator end charts. Write $M_O,M_X$ and $A_G=(M_O-M_X)/2-(n-1)/2$ for the grid grading functions. For every actual continuous Whitney class $\phi:x\to y$ in $\operatorname{Sym}^n(T)$, define its domain and marked multiplicities by the relative point-divisor degrees of any smooth model. Its actual fixed-end Fredholm index $\mu(\phi)$, before source translation, satisfies
$$\mu(\phi)=M_O(x)-M_O(y)+2\sum_{i=1}^n n_{O_i}(\phi),$$
and
$$A_G(x)-A_G(y)=\sum_{i=1}^n n_{X_i}(\phi)-\sum_{i=1}^n n_{O_i}(\phi).$$
These identities hold for all realized classes, with positive, zero or negative marked multiplicities. In particular no condition $n_X=0$ is imposed. They remain valid for the actual linearized index of a smooth finite-energy holomorphic strip with generator ends and the protected product end data, under the auxiliary complex-structure homotopies in the suppliers.

Consequently, an actual index-one holomorphic strip counted with weight $\prod_i U_i^{n_{O_i}}$, if all its marked multiplicities are nonnegative, lowers $M_O$ by one and drops the $A_G$ filtration by exactly $\sum_i n_{X_i}$, when $U_i$ has bidegree $(-2,-1)$. This is the full filtered relative grading assertion, rather than only its zero-$X$ associated graded specialization. It does not assert existence or finiteness of counts, square-zero, move invariance, a grid-to-analytic equivalence, or identification of an absolute analytic grading normalization.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $R=\{z=x+iy:0<x<a,\ 0<y<b\}$, $a,b>0$. There is a proper holomorphic map $p:R\to\{s+it:0<t<1\}$ of degree two, unique up to a real additive constant among such maps whose imaginary part is bounded with limiting values zero on the two open horizontal sides and one on the two open vertical sides. It is explicitly
$$p(z)=\frac4\pi\sum_{\substack{k\ge1\\k\text{ odd}}}\frac{\sinh(k\pi(z-a/2)/b)}{k\cosh(k\pi a/(2b))}.$$
The southwest and northeast corners tend to the negative strip end, and the other two corners to the positive end. In their inward corner coordinates, $p$ has logarithmic leading coefficient $2/\pi$ at the negative ends and $-2/\pi$ at the positive ends, with a holomorphic remainder. The corresponding end coordinates $e^{\pi p/2}$ and $e^{-\pi p/2}$ have nonzero first derivative at those corners. It extends across every open side by reflection, and has exactly one interior simple branch point. No general conformal-mapping theorem or full Axiom of Choice is used.

Let $\Sigma$ be a closed Riemann surface, $m\ge1$, and $p\in\Sigma$. In the complex symmetric product $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ let $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. Let $L_0,L_1\subset X$ be compact submanifolds disjoint from $E_p$. Suppose $J_t$ agrees with the fixed complex structure of $X$ on one neighborhood of $E_p$ for every $t\in[0,1]$. Let $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ be a smooth solution of $\partial_\tau u+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$, with boundary on $L_0,L_1$ and uniform limits as $\tau\to\pm\infty$ at points of $L_0\cap L_1$.

The intersections of $u$ with $E_p$ are a finite collection of interior points, each with positive integral local intersection multiplicity. Their sum is nonnegative, and it is zero exactly when $u$ avoids $E_p$. In pointed Heegaard data, with $L_0,L_1$ the product tori and $p$ any marked point, this proves nonnegativity of the domain multiplicity $n_p(u)$ whenever it is defined by intersection with $E_p$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected Riemann surface, $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ with its standard complex structure, and $m\ge1$. For $a\in\Sigma$ put $E_a=\{a\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. This is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at repeated tuples. The universal incidence hypersurface $\mathcal E=\{(a,D):D\in E_a\}\subset\Sigma\times X$ carries a smooth complex divisor line bundle with its canonical section, whose zero set is $\mathcal E$ with multiplicity one.

For a smooth map $v:S\to X$, where $S$ is an oriented sphere or a closed disk, define $n_a(v)$ as the degree of the pullback point-divisor line bundle; for a disk use the canonical section to trivialize it on the boundary, and require $v(\partial S)\cap E_a=\varnothing$. The proof constructs this integer by elementary frame winding. It is defined even when a sphere lies wholly in $E_a$.

For a sphere, $n_a(v)$ is independent of $a$ on all of $\Sigma$. For a disk whose boundary tuples have all entries in a finite union of curves $\Gamma\subset\Sigma$, it is independent of $a$ on each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus\Gamma$. If $v^{-1}(E_a)$ is finite and the map is holomorphic on a neighborhood of every one of these points, then
$$n_a(v)=\sum_{z\in v^{-1}(E_a)}\operatorname{ord}_z(F_a\circ v)\ge0,$$
where $F_a$ is any local holomorphic defining function of the smooth hypersurface $E_a$. Each term is a positive integer. Thus the degree agrees with proper holomorphic intersection multiplicity, while divisor containment is handled by its degree definition and actual point movement rather than an unsupported proper-intersection assumption.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $C$ be a connected closed Riemann surface, $\Sigma$ a closed Riemann surface, and $u:C\to\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ holomorphic for the standard complex symmetric-product structure, $m\ge1$. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ be the quotient. No assumption that the image avoids or is not contained in the repeated-point locus is made.

There are a finite set $B\subset C$, a positive integer $d\le m!$, a compact possibly disconnected Riemann surface $F$, a degree-$d$ holomorphic branched covering $p:F\to C$, and a holomorphic map $\widetilde u:F\to\Sigma^m$ with
$$q\circ\widetilde u=u\circ p.$$
Over $C\setminus B$ the covering is unbranched and its fiber is exactly the finite set of distinct orderings of the tuple $u(z)$, including its repeated entries. Near every point above $B$, in suitable source coordinates the map $p$ is $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^r$ for an integer $r\ge1$, and all coordinate maps of $\widetilde u$ extend holomorphically through $\zeta=0$. In particular this lift exists for a curve lying wholly in the diagonal, including nonreduced tuples with a fixed repeated coordinate.

The proof also gives the following local fact. A monic polynomial with holomorphic one-variable coefficient germs admits, on a sufficiently small punctured disk, a locally holomorphic collection of distinct roots with constant multiplicities. Those roots extend holomorphically after finite monodromy power substitutions, even when the original polynomial has an identically vanishing discriminant.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a smooth real rank-$2m$ vector bundle on $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$, $m\ge1$, with a smooth endomorphism $J$ satisfying $J^2=-I$. On the two boundary edges let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth real rank-$m$ subbundles with $F_j\cap JF_j=0$. Suppose that outside a compact strip there are specified smooth complex frames $\tau_\pm:\mathbb C^m\to E$, intertwining $i$ and $J$, in which $F_0=\mathbb R^m$ and $F_1=i\mathbb R^m$. Let $P$ be a smooth real linear first-order operator on sections of $E$ with symbol
$$P(f\xi)=fP\xi+f_s\xi+f_tJ\xi$$
for every smooth real function $f$, and suppose its expression in each end frame is exactly $\partial_s+i\partial_t$ outside a compact strip.

There exist a global smooth complex frame $\Phi$, a sign matrix $S_+=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,1,\ldots,1)$ with $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$, an integer $\ell$, and a smooth real function $\vartheta(s)$, constant at $\pi/2$ on the negative end and $\pi/2+\ell\pi$ on the positive end, such that $\Phi=\tau_-$ on the negative end, $\Phi=\tau_+S_+$ on the positive end, and
$$F_0=\Phi\mathbb R^m,\qquad F_1=\Phi\left(e^{i\vartheta(s)}\mathbb R\times i\mathbb R^{m-1}\right).$$
In this frame $P$ is $\partial_s+i\partial_t+B(s,t)$ with smooth compactly supported real linear $B$. On the $H^1$ completion of compactly supported smooth sections satisfying those actual boundary subbundles, with the norm defined by finite bundle charts on a compact core and the prescribed frames on the ends, $P$ maps to the corresponding $L^2(E)$ space and is real Fredholm, with
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}P=-\ell.$$
The same index holds with the weight $e^{\delta|s|}$ for $0\le\delta<\pi/2$. These are indices before any translation quotient. The integer $\ell$ is independent of the choices in the construction, since it is minus the index of this fixed operator.

In particular the conclusion applies to the actual linearization at a smooth $J_t$-holomorphic strip of finite Dirichlet energy, measured in a smooth target metric, in a compact target, with compact totally real boundary submanifolds of transverse finite intersection, whenever the chosen target charts at their intersections identify those submanifolds with $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t$ with the constant structure $i$ for every $t$. For product Heegaard tori such a geometric choice is available by the product-integrable generator-neighborhood construction. No domain Euler-measure formula, corner/excision theorem, generic regularity, or moduli count is part of this conclusion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$, $m\ge1$, and $0<\theta_j<\pi$. Write $X_0=H^1_\theta$ for the real $H^1$ completion of smooth maps compactly supported in $s$ satisfying $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$ and $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $B:S\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb C^m)$ be smooth up to the boundary, with every derivative bounded, and suppose its uniform end limits are real diagonal matrices $\operatorname{diag}(b_{\pm,j})$ with $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}\notin\pi\mathbb Z$. For an integer $q\ge0$ put
$$X_q=H^{q+1}(S;\mathbb C^m)\cap X_0,\qquad Y_q=H^q(S;\mathbb C^m),\qquad T_q=\partial_s+i\partial_t+B:X_q\longrightarrow Y_q,$$
using real Hilbert spaces and their indicated Sobolev norms. There are no higher boundary conditions: only the zeroth trace encoded by $X_0$ is required. In particular no normal derivative or forcing trace is prescribed.

Every $T_q$ is bounded Fredholm. Its kernel is the same set as the kernel of $T_0$, and its range is $Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}T_0$. The inclusion of $Y_q$ in $L^2$ induces an isomorphism of real cokernels. Thus
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}T_q=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}T_0=\sum_j\left(\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{-,j}}\pi\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{+,j}}\pi\right\rfloor\right).$$
More precisely, if $u\in X_0$ and $T_0u=f\in H^q$, then $u\in X_q$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q\bigl(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|u\|_{H^1}\bigr).$$

The same conclusions hold with smooth two-sided weights $w=e^{\delta\rho(s)}$, where $\rho$ is smooth, equals $|s|$ outside a compact interval, has all derivatives of positive order bounded, and $0\le\delta<\min_{\pm,j,n}|\pi n-\theta_j+b_{\pm,j}|$. Weighted spaces mean $wu\in X_q$ and $wf\in Y_q$. Their index is the same displayed index. The weight is smooth at zero even for $q\ge1$.

Finally, for an actual geometric strip operator with exact product-integrable ends and the smooth bundle frame supplied by the geometric strip normal-form theorem, the actual $H^{q+1}$ boundary-section domain and $H^q$ target have this same real index before translation quotient, also with these smooth weights. This asserts integer Hilbert Sobolev agreement; no $W^{1,p}$ comparison or Heegaard-domain Euler formula is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and the actual finite-energy half-strip hypotheses of [[lem-finite-energy-transverse-strip-end-convergence]]. Suppose additionally that at each point $x\in L_0\cap L_1$ there is a smooth target coordinate chart $q_x$ centered at $x$, taking the two boundary submanifolds locally to
$$\mathbb R^m,\qquad \prod_{j=1}^m e^{i\theta_j(x)}\mathbb R,\qquad 0<\theta_j(x)<\pi,$$
and taking $J(s,t,\cdot)$ to the constant structure $i$ throughout that neighborhood for all source $s,t$. These are concrete geometric choice hypotheses, not moduli-space axioms.

Let $x_+$ be the end limit. On a sufficiently far tail put $v=q_{x_+}\circ u$ and $\gamma_+=\min_j(\pi-\theta_j(x_+))>0$. For every integer $k\ge0$ there is $C_k<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le1}|D^k v(s,t)|\le C_k e^{-\gamma_+s}.$$
For every $0\le\delta<\gamma_+$ and every finite $k$, the map $e^{\delta s}v$ belongs to $H^k$ on a far tail. Thus all derivatives converge exponentially to the constant generator. Constructing the prescribed coordinate charts and an admissible global $J$ with these values is a separate prerequisite.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $m\ge1$ and angles $0<\theta_j<\pi$ for $1\le j\le m$. On the strip $S=\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ impose the real product-plane boundary conditions $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$ and $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $H^1_\theta$ be the completion of smooth maps satisfying these conditions and compactly supported in the $s$ direction, for the norm
$$\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|u_s\|_2^2+\|u_t\|_2^2.$$
The real linear operator $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t$ extends to an isomorphism $H^1_\theta\to L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$. Put $\gamma=\min_j\{\theta_j,\pi-\theta_j\}>0$. Its inverse satisfies
$$\|D^{-1}f\|_2\le\gamma^{-1}\|f\|_2,\qquad \|D^{-1}f\|_{H^1}\le\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}\,\|f\|_2.$$
For $0\le\delta<\gamma$, set $w(s)=e^{\delta|s|}$, $H^1_{\theta,\delta}=\{u:wu\in H^1_\theta\}$ with norm $\|wu\|_{H^1}$, and $L^2_\delta=\{f:wf\in L^2\}$ with norm $\|wf\|_2$. Then $D:H^1_{\theta,\delta}\to L^2_\delta$ is an isomorphism and
$$\|D^{-1}f\|_{H^1_{\theta,\delta}}\le\frac{\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}}{1-\delta/\gamma}\,\|f\|_{L^2_\delta},\qquad \|wD^{-1}f\|_2\le\frac{\|wf\|_2}{\gamma-\delta}.$$
These are estimates for the constant linear asymptotic model. They make no assertion about nonlinear strip decay, a variable-coefficient operator, or its Maslov index.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(\Sigma,j)$ be a closed Riemann surface with positive area form $\eta$, and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$, $m\ge1$, with its induced complex structure $J_0$. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to X$ be the quotient, $\Delta\subset X$ its repeated-point locus, and $\Omega=\sum_{l=1}^m\operatorname{pr}_l^*\eta$. Off $\Delta$ the permutation-invariant form $\Omega$ descends to a smooth form $\omega$ on $X\setminus\Delta$. Equip $X$ with any smooth Riemannian metric $g$.

Let $L_\alpha,L_\beta$ be product tori formed from two finite systems of pairwise disjoint attaching curves, with transverse intersections between the systems. Suppose a smooth path $J_t$ agrees with $J_0$ on a neighborhood $V$ of $\Delta$ and tames $\omega$ on $X\setminus V$. Let $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ be a smooth $J_t$-holomorphic strip, with boundary on these tori, finite $g$-Dirichlet energy, and uniform limits at both ends to intersection generators. For each complementary region $R$ of the attaching curves write $n_R(u)$ for the signed intersection multiplicity of $u$ with $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ at a generic $p\in R$.

There is a constant $C$ depending only on the fixed geometric data and the path, independent of $u$, such that
$$E_g(u)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R\times[0,1]}(|u_s|_g^2+|u_t|_g^2)\,dsdt\le C\sum_R n_R(u)\int_R\eta.$$
In particular energies of all such representatives with one fixed domain are uniformly bounded. The finite-energy hypothesis here is explicit; no assertion that arbitrary asymptotically convergent smooth solutions automatically have finite energy is included.

Let $\Omega$ be a complex domain and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be harmonic.

1. If $u$ has an interior local maximum or an interior local minimum, then $u$
   is constant on $\Omega$.
2. If $\Omega$ is bounded and $u$ extends continuously to $\overline{\Omega}$,
   then
   $$\sup_{\overline{\Omega}}u=\sup_{\partial\Omega}u,\qquad \inf_{\overline{\Omega}}u=\inf_{\partial\Omega}u.$$

The **grid-complex algorithm** takes a finite encoded grid and a mode from $\{\mathrm{tilde},\mathrm{minus\text{-}associated\text{-}graded},\mathrm{minus\text{-}filtered}\}$. It requires an integer grid number $n\ge2$, disjoint $O$- and $X$-markings with exactly one of each in every row and column, and an induced component permutation that is one $n$-cycle. If $n<2$ or the marking conditions fail, return `invalid-grid`; if the component permutation has more than one cycle, return `link-input-not-supported`. No chain complex is returned on either branch.

For a valid knot grid, number the horizontal and vertical circles $1,\ldots,n$ and enumerate all permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ in lexicographic order. The state for a permutation $\sigma$ consists of the $n$ intersections $(i,\sigma(i))$. For each ordered pair of states $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$, if they agree in other than exactly $n-2$ points, add no rectangle terms. Otherwise enumerate the at most two torus rectangles with the four nonshared state points as corners, retain those whose interiors contain no point of $\mathbf x$, and apply the selected mode. In the full filtered mode, each term drops filtration by $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$; the associated-graded mode retains precisely the terms with zero drop, which are the rectangles with no $X$-marking:

1. **Tilde mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2$. Count a retained rectangle with coefficient $1$ exactly when its interior contains no $O$- or $X$-marking.
2. **Associated-graded minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count a retained rectangle exactly when its interior contains no $X$-marking, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$.
3. **Full filtered minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count every retained rectangle, regardless of its $X$-markings, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$. Use the grid Alexander value for each state and assign filtration drop $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$ to this term.

Return the ordered state list, the mode and coefficient ring, the exact differential matrix obtained by summing coefficients modulo two, the state Maslov and Alexander values, and the filtration data for the full filtered mode. The algorithm returns this finite presentation only; its identification with knot Floer homology and its independence of the chosen grid are separate theorems. The factor $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ is not multiplied into the output.

For every one-component toroidal grid and each of the tilde, associated-graded minus, and full filtered minus modes, the differential defined by the grid-complex algorithm satisfies $\partial^2=0$ over its stated coefficient ring.

derivations.claim: First record the actual incidence construction needed for integrable strips, rather than import a clean-cover hypothesis. The two compact product tori avoid the diagonal, and the generator ends do too. Thus an actual strip with uniform generator ends meets the diagonal only in a compact interior part. Holomorphic local discriminants make this intersection discrete unless the whole map lies in the diagonal; the latter is excluded by its boundary. It is therefore finite. Off those points order its distinct roots locally. Their continuations give the finite degree-$n$ root-label cover of the punctured base, with monodromy permutations of the $n$ labels. At each omitted point separate its permutation into cycles of lengths $r$. In a cycle use the positive source coordinate $b-b_0=\zeta^r$; each root is now a single bounded holomorphic function of $\zeta$, and extends across zero. Bounded holomorphic removal follows directly from its Cauchy coefficients: every negative Laurent coefficient has absolute value at most $M\rho^{|k|}$ and vanishes as $\rho\to0$. This is the local construction in [F3], applied here to the actual strip. Near a physical boundary the roots are distinct and lie on their labelled straight row or column, so they extend by ordinary real-line Schwarz reflection; reflection follows by conjugating the upper and lower holomorphic pieces, whose matching real traces cancel the interface term, and the Cauchy integral formula. At the two ends, each distinct root has the exact transverse Fourier expansion in [F4]; in the quadrant coordinate $q=e^{\pi(s+it)/2}$, or $q=e^{-\pi(s+it)/2}$ at the other end, it is a convergent series of odd nonnegative powers with its generator constant.
